newsitem.title: USA: Most of N.Dakota gears up for spring wheat seeding.
newsitem.headline: Most of N.Dakota gears up for spring wheat seeding.

text.p: Spring wheat plantings in North Dakota look set to be delayed in the northeast and Red River Valley counties this year but elsewhere in the state prospects appear favorable, a leading agronomist said.

"For the most part, fields in central and western North Dakota are definitely going to get a much earlier start (to plantings) than the last two years if this weather pattern continues," said Kent McKay of North Dakota State University.
McKay said he was, however, predicting later than normal planting in the northeast and Red River Valley counties.
The spring wheat areas of the Dakotas and Minnesota should remain dry and cool through late this week, meteorologists said on Wednesday.
McKay said farmers in much North Dakota were already completing planting preparations, two weeks earlier than the last two years.
"Overall we are not projecting any major delays so statewide we are still in pretty good shape," McKay said.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture's March planting survey forecast a cut in North Dakota's hard red spring wheat acreage of 20 percent to 7.7 milllion acres.
Soybean acres in the state were seen rising 35 percent to 1.1 million.
McKay said the overall planting outlook for the state had probably changed little since then.

"We are not going to see much more of a decrease in wheat acres," McKay said, noting he had received numerous calls from farmers in western North Dakota who were considering planting more wheat following the recent strength of prices.
"It could offset any declines in acres due to the flooding in the east," McKay said of possible expanded plantings in other areas.

Figures issued by the North Dakota Agricultural Statistics Service show in 1996 about 1.79 million acres were planted to spring wheat in counties bordering the Red River, representing 19 percent of the state's 9.6 million acre plantings.

McKay said planting delays in the Red River Valley would probably not lead to much increase in soybean area, even though it can normally be sown later than wheat, partly due to the large amount of sugarbeets grown in the region.

"Some of the fields designated for wheat are probably going to stay wheat because of their sugarbeet rotation," he said, noting that there was a danger of some disease crossover between sugarbeets and soybeans.

Scott Stofferahn, state executive director of the Farm Service Agency in North Dakota said the amount of land under water in the state was now probably higher than the 1.7 million acre estimate issued by FSA just over a week ago.
He also said the area between the Red River and the Missouri River had a lot of ponding in fields.

"There is an awful lot of water standing there that we are going to have to contend with for some time to come," he said, noting the area west of the Missouri River was well drained and had no problems with ponding.
USDA on Monday said three percent of overall U.S. spring wheat had been planted as of Sunday, slightly behind four percent a year ago, and well behind the five-year average of 13 percent.
